summary: Discovery call to map Cirrus Tech's model selection needs across hosted, dedicated and private options. Key drivers: long context for multi-document summarization (target up to 32k tokens), multilingual support (EN+ES+PT), tool-calling for internal data connectors, and strict data residency/KMS requirements. Redwood AE+SE overviewed open-model tradeoffs (Llama-family variants, Mistral, Mosaic, LLMs trimmed for FP16/quant), discussed batching, KV cache and quantization impacts, and proposed benchmarks and a pilot plan.
topics: Open model comparison and quantization tradeoffs
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) decision factors
Tool-calling (secure connectors) and function calling patterns
Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS/HSM, data residency
transcript:
00:00 Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
00:06 Marta (Cirrus): Hi, Marta here.
00:08 David (Cirrus CTO): David on my side.
00:10 Lee (Infra): Lee here.
00:12 Anika (PM): Anika.
00:15 Priya (Redwood SE): Priya from Redwood. Good to meet you all.
00:18 Jordan: Quick agenda - understand your workloads, context length needs, multilingual and tool-calling, then map to hosted/dedicated/private tradeoffs. Sounds good?
00:28 Marta: Yep, that's perfect. We're trying to decide if we'll start on hosted for speed, or go straight to dedicated or private because of compliance and some low-latency requirements.
00:40 David: Our main use case is multi-doc summarization for enterprise support tickets and contracts, often stitched together. We can easily hit 20k-30k token contexts, sometimes more. Latency target is sub-1s for short answers, but for the long summarizations we tolerate higher. Cost is obviously a factor.
01:05 Priya: Thanks, that's helpful. A couple clarifying q's — when you say 20k-30k tokens, is that single contiguous context or many concatenated docs with metadata and vector lookup?
01:18 David: It's concatenated — we batch up the doc chunks with some retrieved context from embeddings. There's also tool-calling where the model queries internal APIs and then formats the answer.
01:30 Lee: From infra, we need to make sure keys don't leave our cloud account and that logs are auditable; KMS and HSM might be necessary.
01:38 Jordan: Understood. On model selection: open-models give you flexibility but different families behave differently at extended context lengths. Roughly, Llama 3 variants are strong at instruction following and have decent tool-calling, Mistral-like weights are compute efficient, and some Mosaic/Mistral hybrids do well with quantization. But it depends on your exact prompts.
02:00 Marta: We're particularly worried about hallucinations when the context is huge and when invoking tools — we need deterministic grounding.
02:08 Priya: Right, that's where structured tool-calling and function signatures help — enforce response schemas and validate. Also prefix/KV cache can reduce repeated token cost and improve latency on repeated user flows.
02:18 David: Can you say more about KV cache — we've heard the term but not fully sure of the operational implications.
02:24 Priya: Sure, so KV (key-value) cache holds previous attention key/value states for autoregressive decoding; on long dialogs or long contexts, if you reuse earlier segments it avoids re-encoding them. It's also helpful for streaming and low-latency incremental generation. Two caveats — memory footprint spikes for very long contexts, and not all quantized runtimes preserve identical KV semantics, so we test per model.
02:50 Jordan: On deployment modes — Hosted is fastest to get running, cost-effective for low to medium qps, and we handle model ops and upgrades. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and isolation, with reserved GPU pools. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict security or data residency — gives you full control but has higher ops overhead.
03:10 Lee: If we do Private, do we need to manage HSM ourselves or can you integrate with our cloud KMS?
03:16 Priya: We integrate with major cloud KMS and support HSM-backed keys. For on-prem HSM we have patterns but there's an extra engineering phase. We'll scope that in a security deep-dive.
03:28 Marta: Model accuracy is critical. Which open models would you shortlist for 32k contexts and multilingual Spanish/Portuguese?
03:36 Priya: Shortlist I'd propose: Llama-3-32k (if available in a quantized high-ctx variant), Mistral-Extended (we've seen tuned forks), and a Mosaic-family 32k tuned model. Also evaluate long-context fine-tuned variants — some teams do chunking + reranker + sliding window to reduce hallucinations. We should test a retrieval-augmented pipeline vs single long-context.
04:00 David: How about tool-calling? We need structured outputs that call internal APIs and assert permissions. Does Redwood support function-calling and role-based API keys per tool?
04:08 Jordan: Yes — function-calling is supported at the API level and the Redwood Console lets you manage per-route tokens and RBAC. You can restrict which routes a tool can call and tie that to per-customer service tokens.
04:20 Lee: Any limits on embedding store integrations — we use an internal vector DB behind an API.
04:25 Priya: We commonly integrate with an internal vector DB via secure connector; tool-calls can proxy to that DB. We recommend limiting returned context size and passing canonicalized passages to the model.
04:36 Anika: On cost — can you outline cost differences between using a large 32k model hosted vs using a 8k model with retrieval?
04:44 Jordan: Roughly, serving a 32k-context model at high token lengths increases per-inference compute and memory; cost per request can be 2–4x a tiled 8k model with retrieval, depending on sequence lengths and batching. But retrieval adds infra and latency complexity. We'll send a cost comparison table.
05:02 Marta: We need multilingual quality parity — Spanish & Portuguese are musts. Some open models degrade. Any quick guidance?
05:10 Priya: Generally, large multilingual or instruction-tuned LLMs do better. Llama variants fine-tuned with multilingual datasets perform stronger. We'll run bilingual evals on your sample prompts. Also watch tokenization: some models tokenize non-English less efficiently which raises token counts and cost.
05:30 David: What about quantization? We want cost savings but worried about quality loss on long contexts.
05:36 Priya: 4-bit quantization is common and can preserve quality for many tasks, but at large context sizes you need runtime support that keeps KV cache precision. We often recommend mixed approach: quantize for most traffic, use higher-precision instances for latency-sensitive or high-context generations. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles by workload.
06:00 Jordan: Any regulatory constraints? Marta: EU data residency for EU accounts, SOC 2 is required, and we need immutable audit logs for calls for some customers.
06:08 Priya: We provide audit logs and per-token trace data in the console; retention can be configured or sent to your log archive. For Private deployments, logs can remain inside your VPC.
06:20 Lee: From infra — what's typical throughput for dedicated pools? If we need bursts of 200 qps with mostly short responses and occasional long 30k requests, can the autoscaling handle that?
06:32 Jordan: Dedicated pools support configurable autoscaling and burst capacity. Typical pattern is reserve enough headroom for predictable baseline and enable burst policies — long 30k requests often use different instance types and scheduling policies so they don't block short-request queues. We'll propose a config based on your qps profile.
06:50 David: Can Redwood help with model rollouts and canary tests?
06:54 Priya: Yes — Console supports canary rollouts, A/B, and automatic fallback to smaller models if latency SLOs are missed. Also includes quality monitoring tied to prompt sets.
07:08 Marta: Let's talk benchmarks — what do you need from us to run a meaningful bench?
07:12 Priya: A representative prompt set, expected concurrency patterns, desired latency SLOs per route, and any constraints like data residency. Also clarify which languages to include and tool-calling examples. Ideally a sample of 200–500 prompts covering short, medium, and long contexts.
07:30 Anika: We'll provide that.
07:32 Jordan: Great. A couple quick technical notes: for long contexts, sometimes chunking plus a reranker reduces hallucinations and cost. Also consider hybrid approach: hosted for dev and dedicated for production with reserved capacity if you have predictable throughput.
07:48 David: Are there customers doing private on-prem with Redwood?
07:52 Priya: Yes, a few regulated customers run private control planes with on-prem inference. There's an initial engineering phase for networking and KMS but we have a playbook.
08:02 Lee: Any callouts about streaming and partial results with tool-calling? We need to stream partial answers while tool calls are executed.
08:10 Priya: Streaming works; function-calls can be triggered and you can emit partial structured drafts while the connector runs. You want to design idempotent tool endpoints and include timeouts and fallbacks.
08:22 Jordan: I'm hearing the top priorities: 1) validate 32k-context model behavior and cost 2) multilingual parity (EN/ES/PT) 3) secure tool-calling with KMS/HSM + audit logs 4) pilot plan with benchmarks and recommended deployment mode. Is that right?
08:36 Marta: Yes. Also minimize hallucinations in the tool-calling flows.
08:40 David: And quantify cost tradeoffs between hosted and dedicated esp vs reserved GPU commits.
08:45 Priya: We'll include a cost model.
09:00 Marta: One more — what about offline batch summarization (nightly jobs) where we process large corpuses? Could that run on cheaper quantized infra?
09:08 Priya: Absolutely — offline batch is a great candidate for aggressive quantization and lower-cost instances. We can separate online SLO-bound traffic from offline batch in routing policies.
09:18 Jordan: I'll put some initial numbers on reserved capacity vs on-demand and include a pilot timeline in the follow-up.
09:25 Anika: Timeline wise, we'd like a pilot in early January — internal procurement cycles end mid-December.
09:32 Jordan: Good to know. We'll aim to have benchmark results and a pilot proposal before year-end.
09:38 Lee: Slightly worried about egress and network costs in Hosted. If we process EU-only data, does Hosted route through EU endpoints?
09:45 Priya: Yes, Hosted regions can be selected by customer; data residency and region routing are supported. For strict residency, Private/VPC is recommended.
10:00 Marta: Any red flags we should know about when moving forward?
10:04 Priya: Tests we run often surface tokenization inefficiencies for certain languages; some long-context variants need tuning. Also, tool-calling needs careful auth modeling. No showstopper, just engineering work.
10:18 Jordan: I'll recap at the end but quick question — do you have a preferred shortlist of models you want us to evaluate first?
10:24 Marta: We don't have one yet. We want Redwood to propose 3-4 candidates for each path (hosted/quantized vs high-precision).
10:32 Jordan: Great. We'll propose: Llama-3-32k (quant + hp), Mistral-Extended-32k, and a Mosaic long-context tuned variant, plus a smaller 8k retrieval-enabled setup as a cost-optimized baseline.
10:50 David: For tool-calling security — can function calls be audited with payload redaction? We need PII removed from logs.
10:58 Priya: Yes, Redwood supports log redaction rules and you can configure which fields are retained. For Private, log retention can be entirely under your control.
11:12 Anika: Procurement will ask about SLA — do you offer any uptime SLAs for Dedicated?
11:18 Jordan: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets with enterprise contracts. We'll include the SLA template.
11:26 Marta: OK, can you also include sample benchmarking scripts so our infra team can reproduce tests?
11:30 Priya: We'll include an executable bench harness and sample config.
11:36 Jordan: Anything else before we wrap?
11:40 David: No, looks good.
11:42 Jordan: Alright quick recap — action items and next steps we'll email: benchmark plan, model shortlist, cost comparison, security playbook and schedule a security deep-dive. Thanks everyone.
11:55 Marta: Thanks all.
11:58 End of recording.
